Atlas & Cloud Setup: MongoDB Atlas offers free M0 clusters, auto-scaling, backups, monitoring, global clusters, serverless instances, and Atlas Search. Provision via web UI, API, or Terraform.

# Create Atlas cluster via API
curl -s -u "publicKey:privateKey" \
  --digest https://cloud.mongodb.com/api/atlas/v1.0/groups/{groupId}/clusters \
  -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"MyCluster","providerSettings":{"providerName":"AWS","regionName":"us-east-1","instanceSizeName":"M10"}}'
BSON Types Deep: BSON extends JSON with types: ObjectId (12-byte unique id), Date (64-bit millisecond timestamp), NumberInt/NumberLong, Decimal128 (exact precision), Binary, Regex, Code, Timestamp, and MinKey/MaxKey for comparison.

db.typesDemo.insertOne({
  _id: ObjectId(),
  intVal: NumberInt(42),
  longVal: NumberLong(9999999999),
  decVal: NumberDecimal('19.99'),
  dateVal: new Date(),
  binaryVal: BinData(0, 'S2V5cw=='),
  regexVal: /search.*term/i,
  tsVal: Timestamp({ t: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000), i: 1 })
})
Connection Strings: Standard format: `mongodb://host:port/db`. Atlas SRV format: `mongodb+srv://cluster.mongodb.net/db`. Options: retryWrites, w, readPreference, maxPoolSize, connectTimeoutMS, tls.

# Standard
mongodb://localhost:27017/myDB
# With auth
mongodb://user:pass@host1:27017,host2:27017/myDB?replicaSet=rs0
# Atlas SRV
mongodb+srv://myUser:myPass@cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net/sales?retryWrites=true&w=majority
# Pool options
mongodb://localhost:27017/myDB?maxPoolSize=50&connectTimeoutMS=5000
What is MongoDB: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like BSON documents. It's schema-less, horizontally scalable, and designed for modern applications with dynamic data models. Supports replica sets for HA and sharding for distributed data.
MongoDB Versions & Editions: MongoDB 7.0+ (latest) with improved queryable encryption, change streams, and aggregation. Editions: Community (free), Enterprise (advanced security, auditing, Ops Manager), and Atlas (cloud-managed).
mongosh Scripting: mongosh supports full JavaScript scripting with variables, loops, functions, and print helpers. Write scripts and load them with `load()`. The `--eval` flag runs inline expressions.
Document Model Deep Dive: Documents are JSON-like structures with field-value pairs. Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, nested objects, dates, ObjectIds, and more. Max document size is 16MB. Nested fields use dot notation for access.

Comparison Operators: `$eq`, `$ne`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$in`, `$nin`. Combine multiple on the same field. `$in` accepts an array of values. Use `$ne` and `$nin` with indexes carefully (they scan broadly).

db.products.find({ price: { $gte: 10, $lte: 100 } })
db.products.find({ category: { $in: ['Electronics', 'Books'] } })
db.orders.find({ status: { $ne: 'cancelled' }, total: { $gte: 50 } })
Logical Operators: `$and`, `$or`, `$not`, `$nor`. Implicit AND is used for comma-separated conditions. Use explicit `$and` when conditions involve the same field or complex expressions.
Array Operators: `$all` matches arrays containing all elements. `$elemMatch` matches docs with an array element satisfying all conditions. `$size` matches exact array length. Combine for precise array queries.
Element & Evaluation Operators: `$exists` checks field presence. `$type` matches BSON type. `$expr` enables aggregation expressions in queries. `$mod` modulo match. `$regex` pattern matching.
$expr & Aggregation Variables: `$expr` allows aggregation expressions in queries. `$$` references system variables (`$NOW`, `$ROOT`). `let` defines variables for use within `$expr`. Enables cross-field comparisons and computed conditions.
Cursor Methods & Projection: Cursors provide `.sort()`, `.limit()`, `.skip()`, `.count()`, `.forEach()`, `.map()`, `.toArray()`. Projection `{ field: 1 }` includes; `{ field: 0 }` excludes. `_id` is included by default.

db.users.find({}, { name: 1, email: 1, _id: 0 })
  .sort({ name: 1 })
  .skip(20)
  .limit(10)
  .forEach(doc => print(doc.name))

// Cursor count (honors skip/limit)
db.orders.find({ status: 'shipped' }).limit(50).count()
Sort & Pagination Patterns: Use `.sort()` with `.skip()`/`.limit()` for pagination (inefficient at scale). For efficient pagination, use range-based with `$lt`/`$gt` on indexed fields. Avoid large skips.
Geospatial Queries: Supports GeoJSON objects (Point, LineString, Polygon). Create a `2dsphere` index for spherical queries. Operators: `$near` (sorted proximity), `$geoWithin` (within shape), `$geoIntersects` (intersects shape).
Text Search Deep: `$text` query operator with `$search` performs full-text search on text-indexed fields. Supports `$language` for stemming, `$caseSensitive`, `$diacriticSensitive`. `$meta: 'textScore'` for relevance ranking.

Update Operators Deep: `$push` adds to array. `$pull` removes matching items. `$addToSet` adds if not present. `$each` pushes multiple. `$position` inserts at index. `$slice` limits array size after push.
arrayFilters & upsert Deep: arrayFilters target specific array elements for update. upsert: true creates a doc if no match is found. Combined, they enable powerful conditional updates on nested arrays.
Create (insertOne / insertMany): `insertOne()` inserts a single document, `insertMany()` inserts multiple in one round-trip. Each document auto-receives an `_id` (ObjectId) if not provided. `insertMany()` is ordered by default; use `{ ordered: false }` to continue on error.
Read (find / findOne): `find()` returns a cursor to matching documents. `findOne()` returns the first matched doc. Filter object selects documents; projection object limits returned fields. Use `.pretty()` for formatted output in shell.
Update (updateOne / updateMany): `updateOne()` updates the first matching doc. `updateMany()` updates all matching docs. Use `$set`, `$unset`, `$inc`, `$push`, `$pull`, and more. The third parameter accepts options like `upsert: true`.
Delete (deleteOne / deleteMany): `deleteOne()` deletes the first match. `deleteMany()` deletes all matches. `drop()` removes the entire collection including indexes. Deletes are permanent — verify filters with `find()` first.

db.users.deleteOne({ status: 'inactive' })
db.users.deleteMany({ lastLogin: { $lt: new Date('2023-01-01') } })
db.tempData.drop()
// Safe delete pattern
const filter = { status: 'pending' }
print('Docs to delete:', db.users.countDocuments(filter))
db.users.deleteMany(filter)
bulkWrite: `bulkWrite()` performs multiple write operations (insert, update, replace, delete) in a single batch. Accepts an array of operation objects. Supports `{ ordered: false }` for parallel execution.
findAndModify: `findOneAndUpdate()`, `findOneAndDelete()`, `findOneAndReplace()` atomically find and modify a document. Options: `returnDocument: 'after'/'before'`, `sort`, `projection`, `upsert`. Useful for queues and counters.
replaceOne: `replaceOne()` replaces the entire document (except `_id`) matching the filter. Unlike `updateOne()` with `$set`, this replaces all fields. The replacement doc must not contain update operators.
Write Concern: Write concern controls acknowledgment: `w: 0` (fire-and-forget), `w: 1` (primary acknowledged), `w: 'majority'` (majority of nodes), `w: <tag>` (custom tag set). `wtimeout` cancels if not met.

Index Basics: Indexes speed up queries at the cost of write performance and storage. `createIndex()` creates an index. Types: single-field, compound, multikey (array), text, geospatial, hashed. Use `getIndexes()` to inspect.

db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })
db.users.createIndex({ name: 1, age: -1 })
db.orders.createIndex({ tags: 1 }) // multikey (array field)
db.users.getIndexes()
// List all indexes
db.users.getIndexes().forEach(idx => printjson(idx))
Special Index Types: TTL indexes auto-delete docs after a timeout. Sparse indexes skip null fields. Unique indexes enforce uniqueness. Partial indexes index only matching docs. Hidden indexes are not used by the query planner.
Compound Indexes & ESR Rule: Compound indexes support queries on multiple fields. ESR rule: Equality fields first, Sort fields next, Range fields last. Prefix matching — a compound index can serve queries on its leading fields.
Text Indexes: Text indexes enable full-text search with `$text`. A collection can have only one text index (can cover multiple fields). Supports stemming, stop words, weights for field ranking, and text scoring.
Explain & Optimize: `.explain('executionStats')` shows query plans, scanned docs, index usage, and timing. Look for IXSCAN (good) vs COLLSCAN (bad). `winningPlan` shows the chosen plan; `rejectedPlans` shows alternatives.
Index Intersection: MongoDB can use multiple indexes to satisfy a query via index intersection. Use `$or` clauses or compound queries. The query planner evaluates intersection vs compound index to pick the best plan.
Covered Queries: A covered query is fulfilled entirely from the index without reading documents. All queried and projected fields must be in the index. `explain()` shows `FETCH` stage is absent for covered queries.
Index Builds & Rolling Builds: Index builds can block reads/writes on the collection (foreground) or run in background. In replica sets, rolling index builds build on each member sequentially to avoid downtime. For large collections, use `createIndex()` with `{ background: true }`.

Embedding vs Referencing: Embedding stores related data in the same document (fast reads, atomic updates). Referencing stores IDs and uses `$lookup` to join (avoids 16MB limit, reduces duplication). Prefer embedding for one-to-few, referencing for one-to-many.
One-to-One / One-to-Many / Many-to-Many: One-to-one: embed or reference with unique constraint. One-to-many: embed (few) or reference (many). Many-to-many: array of references on either side or a junction collection.
Polymorphic Patterns: Store different entity types in the same collection using a type discriminator field. Common for event sourcing, content management (articles, videos, podcasts), and product catalogs with shared base fields.

db.content.insertMany([
  {
    type: 'article',
    title: 'MongoDB Guide',
    body: 'Content...',
    tags: ['database'],
    wordCount: 1200
  },
  {
    type: 'video',
    title: 'Aggregation Tutorial',
    url: 'https://...',
    duration: 1800,
    resolution: '1080p'
  },
  {
    type: 'podcast',
    title: 'NoSQL Deep Dive',
    audioUrl: 'https://...',
    duration: 3600,
    guests: ['Alice']
  }
])
db.content.createIndex({ type: 1, createdAt: -1 })
Bucket Pattern: The bucket pattern groups related data into time-based or size-based buckets. Ideal for time-series data (IoT sensor readings) — reduces document count, improves index efficiency, and enables pre-aggregation.
Computed & Pre-Aggregation Patterns: Pre-compute aggregates and store them alongside or in separate collections. Use `$merge` for periodic rollups. Reduce computation at read time — ideal for dashboards, leaderboards, and trend analysis.
Document Versioning: Track document versions using a version field or separate history collection. Pattern: store current doc in main collection, append versions to a history collection. Supports rollback and audit trails.
Schema Validation: MongoDB supports JSON Schema validation (`$jsonSchema`) at collection level. Validate required fields, types, ranges, enums, and patterns. Use `validationLevel: 'strict' | 'moderate'` and `validationAction: 'error' | 'warn'`.

Replica Sets Overview: Replica sets provide HA with automatic failover. Primary handles writes; secondaries replicate via oplog. Minimum 3 members (or 2 + arbiter). Use `rs.status()` and `rs.conf()` to monitor.
Replica Set Tags: Tags enable custom write concern and read preference routing. Define tags per member in `rs.conf()`. Use `w: 'majority'` with tag sets to require acknowledgments from specific data centers.
Election Process Deep: Elections occur when primary becomes unreachable. Nodes vote using a protocol based on Raft. The node with highest priority and most up-to-date oplog wins. `settings.electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10s) controls detection speed.
Oplog Size Management: The oplog (local.oplog.rs) is a capped collection recording all writes. Default size: 5% of free disk (min 990MB, max 50GB). If too small, secondaries can fall behind. Resize with `replSetResizeOplog`.
Read Preference Modes: Read preference controls where queries are routed: `primary` (default, strong consistency), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary` (offload reads), `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest` (lowest latency). Use with `maxStalenessSeconds`.
Delayed & Hidden Members: Delayed members replicate data with a time lag (e.g., 1 hour) — protection against accidental drops/corruption. Hidden members are invisible to application queries — used for reporting, backups, or analytics workloads.
Arbiters: An arbiter participates in elections but holds no data. Use to achieve odd-number voting in a 2-node replica set. Never run arbiter on the same server as a data node. Minimum recommended: 3 data nodes instead of 2+arbiter.

Sharding Overview: Sharding horizontally partitions data across shards. Components: mongos (router), config servers (metadata), shards (data). A shard key determines data distribution. Enable per-database, then per-collection.
Shard Key Strategies: Hashed shard keys provide even distribution (good for monotonically increasing fields like ObjectId). Ranged shard keys support range queries but can create hotspots. Zone sharding pins data to specific shards based on key range.
Jumbo Chunks & Balancing: Jumbo chunks exceed the configured chunk size (default 64MB) and cannot be split or moved. Causes: poor shard key cardinality. Balancer migrates chunks between shards. Monitor with `sh.status(true)`.
Shard Zones: Shard zones allow pinning data to specific shards based on shard key ranges. Useful for data residency (GDPR), hot data on fast SSDs, cold data on cheaper storage, and multi-region deployments.

// Tag shards with zone names
sh.addShardTag('shard0000', 'US_East')
sh.addShardTag('shard0001', 'US_West')

// Associate key ranges with zones
sh.updateZoneKeyRange(
  'sales_db.orders',
  { region: 'NY' },
  { region: 'NZ' },
  'US_East'
)
sh.updateZoneKeyRange(
  'sales_db.orders',
  { region: 'CA' },
  { region: 'CZ' },
  'US_West'
)

// Verify zone configuration
sh.status()
Resharding: Resharding changes the shard key of a collection after deployment. MongoDB 7.0+ supports live resharding without downtime. The old key remains until resharding completes. Monitor with `sh.status()`.
mongos Scaling: mongos routers are stateless and can be scaled horizontally. Place mongos close to application servers. Use connection pooling and load balancers in front of multiple mongos instances for HA and throughput.

# Start mongos instances
mongos --configdb configReplSet/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27017
mongos --configdb configReplSet/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27018

# Connection string with multiple mongos
mongodb://mongos1:27017,mongos2:27017,mongos3:27017/mydb?
  loadBalanced=true&retryWrites=true

Atlas Search: Atlas Search is built on Lucene for full-text search. Supports fuzzy matching, autocomplete, synonyms, faceted search, highlighting, and compound queries. Create indexes via web UI or API.
Atlas Data Lake & Federated Query: Atlas Data Lake queries data across Atlas clusters, AWS S3, and Azure Blob Storage using the MongoDB Query API (including aggregation). No data movement — query in place with federated database instances.
Atlas App Services: Atlas App Services (formerly Realm) provides serverless backend: Functions (JS on Atlas), Triggers (DB/webhook/scheduled), GraphQL API, and Data Access Rules. Enables rapid app development without managing servers.
Online Archive & Serverless Instances: Online Archive automatically moves older data to cost-effective S3 storage (fully queryable). Serverless instances scale from 0 to 1M+ ops/sec without capacity planning. Pay per operation.

# Set up online archive (via Atlas CLI)
atlas clusters onlineArchives create --clusterName myCluster \
  --db sales --collection orders \
  --dateField createdAt --archiveAfter 90

# Query archived data (transparent — same queries)
db.orders.find({ createdAt: { $lt: new Date('2023-01-01') } })

# Create serverless instance
atlas clusters create myServerless --provider AWS --region US_EAST_1 \
  --tier SERVERLESS --serverlessBackupOptions enabled=true
Global Clusters & BI Connector: Global clusters distribute data across geographic regions for low-latency reads/writes worldwide. BI Connector (MySQL protocol) enables Tableau, Power BI, and other BI tools to query MongoDB via SQL.

# Global cluster config (via Atlas API)
# Zone-based data distribution
atlas clusters update myCluster \
  --globalClusterConfig '{"customZoneMapping":{"US":"us-east-1","EU":"eu-west-1","APAC":"ap-southeast-1"}}'

// Connection to BI Connector (MySQL port 27016)
mysql -h mycluster.mongodb.net -P 27016 -u myUser -p

// SQL query on MongoDB collections
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) as total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customerId = c._id
WHERE o.createdAt > '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY total DESC;
Atlas Overview & Deployment: Atlas provides fully-managed MongoDB on AWS, Azure, GCP. Free M0 cluster (512MB). Features: auto-scaling, automated backups, monitoring alerts, BI Connector, global clusters, and serverless instances.

# Create cluster via Atlas CLI
atlas clusters create myCluster --provider AWS --region US_EAST_1 --tier M10 --members 3

# Get connection string
atlas clusters connectionString describe myCluster

# Create database user
atlas dbusers create --username appUser --role readWriteAnyDatabase

# Whitelist IP
atlas accessList create --ip 203.0.113.0

MongoDB Driver Deep: Official drivers (Node.js, Python, Java, Go, etc.) provide low-level database access. Key concepts: MongoClient (connection pool), Database, Collection, Cursor. Events: `commandStarted`, `commandSucceeded`, `commandFailed`.
Mongoose Deep (Middleware, Virtuals, Pop: Mongoose provides schema-based modeling with middleware (pre/post hooks for save, validate, find, etc.), virtuals (computed properties), population (reference resolution), plugins, and custom validators.
Change Streams: Change streams provide real-time notifications of data changes (insert, update, replace, delete, drop, invalidate). Can watch a collection, database, or entire cluster. Resumable via resume token.
Transactions: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions (since 4.0). Must use replica set or sharded cluster. Session-based: start a session, execute ops within `withTransaction()`, automatic retry on transient errors.
Retryable Writes: Retryable writes automatically retry write operations on network errors (not on write conflicts). Must use replica set. Enable with `retryWrites=true` in connection string. Idempotent ops are automatically retried.

Atlas Backups: Atlas provides automated backups with configurable retention (1-35 days for M10+). Serverless and M0 have continuous backups. Restore via UI, API, or CLI. Supports point-in-time recovery (PITR) within the retention window.

# Trigger snapshot via Atlas CLI
atlas backups snapshots create --clusterName myCluster --description "pre-upgrade backup"

# List snapshots
atlas backups snapshots list --clusterName myCluster

# Restore snapshot
atlas backups restore start --clusterName myCluster \
  --snapshotId <snapshotId> --targetProjectId <projectId>

# Enable PITR
atlas clusters update myCluster --enablePitr \
  --pitrBackupWindowDays 7

# Restore to point in time
atlas backups restore start --clusterName myCluster \
  --pointInTimeUTCMillis 1704067200000
Ops Manager & On-Premise Backups: Ops Manager (Enterprise) provides automated backup, monitoring, and DB management for on-premise MongoDB. Supports continuous block-level backups with incremental snapshots, queryable backups, and point-in-time recovery.

# Ops Manager backup daemon configuration
# Backup jobs configured via Ops Manager UI

# Command-line backup daemon
mongobackup --backup --destination /data/backups

# Restore from Ops Manager backup
# Via UI: Select snapshot -> Restore -> Target cluster

# Headend restore for fine-grained recovery
# 1. Download snapshot
# 2. Apply oplog
mongorestore --oplogReplay /path/to/oplog/bson
Continuous Backups & PITR: Continuous backups apply oplog entries on top of snapshots for point-in-time recovery within a window. Trade-off: higher storage cost vs granular recovery. PITR allows restoring to any second within the window.

# Enable continuous backup (Atlas)
atlas clusters update myCluster --enablePitr --pitrBackupWindowDays 7

# Ops Manager continuous backup
# Configure via Ops Manager UI > Project > Backup > Continuous

# Restore to a specific timestamp
mongorestore \
  --oplogFile /path/to/oplog.bson \
  --oplogLimit "1704067200:1" \
  --oplogReplay \
  /path/to/snapshot

# Validate backup integrity
mongorestore --dryRun --oplogReplay /path/to/backup
Backup Strategy & Best Practices: Combine snapshot backups (mongodump/Atlas snapshots) with oplog-based continuous backup for PITR. Automate with cron/Ops Manager/Atlas. Test restores regularly. Store backups in different region. Consider compliance retention.

# Weekly full + daily incremental cron
# crontab:
0 3 * * 0  mongodump --uri "$URI" --gzip --archive=/backups/full/$(date +%%Y%%m%%d).gz
0 3 * * 1-6 mongodump --uri "$URI" --gzip --archive=/backups/inc/$(date +%%Y%%m%%d).gz --query '{ "updatedAt": { "$gte": ISODate("'$(date -d '-1 day' +%%Y-%%m-%%d)'") } }'

# Test restore
test_restore() {
  mongorestore --gzip --archive=/backups/full/latest.gz --db test_restore
  if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Backup validated successfully"
    mongosh --eval 'db.getSiblingDB("test_restore").dropDatabase()'
  fi
}
mongodump & mongorestore: `mongodump` creates BSON binary backups. `mongorestore` restores them. Supports `--db`, `--collection`, `--query` (filtered dump), `--gzip`, `--archive`. For consistent backups on replica sets, use `--oplog` or read from secondary.

# Dump entire server
mongodump --uri "mongodb://user:pass@localhost:27017" --out /backup/full

# Dump single database to gzip archive
mongodump --db myDB --gzip --archive=/backup/myDB.gz

# Dump with query filter
mongodump --db myDB --collection orders --query '{ "createdAt": { "$gte": ISODate("2024-01-01") } }' --out /backup/orders

# Point-in-time restore
mongorestore --drop --oplogReplay /backup/full

# Restore from archive
mongorestore --gzip --archive=/backup/myDB.gz --drop

Field Level Encryption: Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE) encrypts fields before they reach the server. Supports deterministic (supports queries) and random (more secure) encryption. Uses a local or remote KMS.
Audit Log: Enterprise feature that logs all auth events, DDL operations, and CRUD operations. Output to console, syslog, JSON file, or BSON. Configure in mongod.conf. Essential for compliance (SOC2, HIPAA, PCI).

# mongod.conf audit configuration
auditLog:
  destination: file
  format: JSON
  path: /var/log/mongodb/audit.log
  filter: '{"atype":{"$in":["authCheck","createCollection","dropCollection","createUser","dropUser"]}}'

# Or via command line
mongod --auditDestination file --auditFormat JSON --auditPath /var/log/mongodb/audit.log

# Parse audit logs
db.adminCommand({ getLog: 'audit' })
TLS/SSL & Network Compression: Enable TLS for encrypted client-server communication. Use PEM certificates. MongoDB supports snappy, zlib, and zstd compression to reduce network bandwidth. Configure both on mongod and client side.

# mongod.conf TLS
net:
  tls:
    mode: requireTLS
    certificateKeyFile: /etc/mongodb/server.pem
    CAFile: /etc/mongodb/ca.pem
    allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: false

# Client connection with TLS
mongosh --tls --tlsCertificateKeyFile client.pem --tlsCAFile ca.pem \
  --host myHost --port 27017

# Connection string with TLS
mongodb://host:27017/db?tls=true&tlsCertificateKeyFile=client.pem&tlsCAFile=ca.pem

# Network compression
mongod --networkMessageCompressors snappy,zstd,zlib
Authentication Methods: MongoDB supports SCRAM (default, password-based), x.509 (certificate), LDAP (enterprise), and Kerberos (enterprise). SCRAM-SHA-256 is the default mechanism, more secure than SCRAM-SHA-1.
Authorization & Roles: Roles define permissions. Built-in: `read`, `readWrite`, `dbAdmin`, `userAdmin`, `clusterAdmin`. Create custom roles with specific actions on specific resources. Use `--auth` flag to enable.
IP Whitelisting & Security Checklist: Bind IP to specific interfaces (not 0.0.0.0). Use firewalls, VPCs, and security groups. Enable `--auth`. Rotate users' passwords. Use SCRAM-SHA-256. Monitor with audit logs. Enable TLS everywhere.

# mongod.conf security best practices
net:
  bindIp: 10.0.0.1,10.0.0.2  # NOT 0.0.0.0
  port: 27017
  tls:
    mode: requireTLS

security:
  authorization: enabled
  javascriptEnabled: false  # disable if not needed

# IP access control list
# Use iptables, AWS SG, etc:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 27017 -s 10.0.0.0/8 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 27017 -j DROP

Aggregation Expressions: Expressions include arithmetic (`$add`, `$multiply`, `$subtract`, `$divide`, `$mod`), string (`$concat`, `$substr`, `$toLower`, `$toUpper`, `$trim`), date (`$year`, `$month`, `$dayOfMonth`, `$dateToString`), and conditional (`$cond`, `$ifNull`, `$switch`).
Accumulators Deep ($first / $last / $pus: `$sum` adds values. `$avg` averages. `$min`/`$max` find extremes. `$first`/`$last` get first/last doc per group (requires sort). `$push` collects into array. `$addToSet` collects unique values.
$lookup (Joins) & $unwind: `$lookup` performs left outer join. `from` is the target collection, `localField` and `foreignField` define the join, `as` names the output array. `$unwind` deconstructs arrays (flattens).
$bucket & $bucketAuto: `$bucket` groups documents into user-defined ranges. `$bucketAuto` auto-generates evenly-sized buckets. Both support `$output` with accumulators. Useful for histograms and distribution analysis.
$facet & $graphLookup: `$facet` runs multiple sub-pipelines on the same input. `$graphLookup` performs recursive graph traversal for hierarchical data like org charts or social networks.
$merge & $out: `$out` writes pipeline results to a new collection (replaces entire collection). `$merge` merges results into an existing collection with merge strategies: `replace`, `merge`, `keepExisting`, `fail`.
$unionWith & $setWindowFields: `$unionWith` combines results from multiple collections (like SQL UNION). `$setWindowFields` enables window functions: `$rank`, `$denseRank`, `$rowNumber`, `$shift`, and sliding window accumulators.
Pipeline Overview & $match / $group: The aggregation pipeline processes documents through a sequence of stages. `$match` filters early (like find). `$group` groups by key and computes accumulators. Always put `$match` early.

Slow Query Analysis: Use `explain('executionStats')` and system.profile to diagnose. Key metrics: `COLLSCAN` (bad, full collection scan), `IXSCAN` (good), `nReturned` vs `totalDocsExamined`, `executionTimeMillis`, and `docsExamined`.
mongostat & mongotop Deep: `mongostat` shows real-time metrics: inserts/sec, queries/sec, page faults, % locked. `mongotop` shows read/write time per collection. Run with `--discover` for replica set monitoring.

# Real-time server stats (every 2s)
mongostat --host localhost:27017 --port 27017 2
# Fields: insert query update delete getmore command %dirty %used flushes vsize   res

# Collection-level read/write activity
mongotop 5
# Fields: ns    total    read    write

# JSON output for parsing
mongostat --host localhost:27017 --json 2

# Discovery mode for replica sets
mongostat --discover --host 'myReplSet/localhost:27017' 2
Connection Pooling: Connection pooling reuses TCP connections to MongoDB. Default pool size is 100 per mongos/mongod. Monitor with `serverStatus().connections`. Tune with `maxPoolSize` and `minPoolSize` in connection string.
WiredTiger Deep & Cache Management: WiredTiger is the default storage engine. It uses a cache (default 50% of RAM - 1GB, min 256MB). Manages data with B-trees and MVCC. Monitor cache hit ratio, evictions, and dirty pages via `serverStatus()`.
Query Profiling: Set profiling level to capture slow queries. Level 0: off. Level 1: queries slower than `slowms`. Level 2: all queries. Results stored in `system.profile`. Analyze for full scans, missing indexes, and sort patterns.
serverStatus & Operation Profiling: `db.serverStatus()` provides comprehensive server metrics: connections, network, operations, memory, locks, wiredTiger cache, and repl info. `db.currentOp()` shows running operations. Kill slow ops with `db.killOp()`.
